headline: ASX slipped 0.5% today as Iran war tensions escalate and lithium weakness hit PLS hard — US markets open tonight.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS copped the biggest hit today, down 3.1% to $4.93. Lithium prices remain under pressure globally — a broader sector selloff as the market continues to weigh oversupply concerns. No company-specific news, but the lithium space is still in a tough rebalancing phase and sentiment is weak.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI fell 1.9% today, dragged down by a soft session across tech-linked stocks on the ASX. No specific negative news for the fund — the AI sector broadly pulled back alongside general market weakness. The fund is now sitting 13.4% below your entry cost.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE slipped 0.8% today. Emerging market stocks tend to be sensitive to global risk appetite, and with US-Iran tensions flaring again, investors are playing it cautious. Nothing structurally wrong here — just broad risk-off sentiment.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS dipped 0.78% today to $536.13, tracking a mild pullback in the underlying US market. This ETF mirrors the entire US share market, so it moves with Wall Street sentiment. Still sitting nearly 4% above your entry cost — a minor day's dip in the context of a solid long-term position.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG edged down 0.5% today — a very minor move for a broadly diversified fund. It holds a mix of Aussie and international shares, so it absorbs daily noise well. Still marginally in the green overall at 0.77% above your entry.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: Lithium pain continues — hold tight
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals dropped another 3.1% today to $4.93, and your position is now 26.9% below cost. Lithium prices remain soft globally due to oversupply — this isn't a Pilbara-specific problem, it's the whole sector. The long-term case for lithium in the energy transition is still intact, but it could stay painful for a while yet. For a long-term holder: hold, don't add just yet until there are clearer signs of price stabilisation.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX: AI ETF softens — long-term thesis unchanged
watch_today.detail: GXAI fell 1.9% today and is 13.4% below your entry cost. Today's dip is about broad market softness, not any specific bad news for AI stocks. Competition is hotting up (Alibaba just launched a laptop-ready AI model to challenge Meta), but the long-term AI growth story remains very much alive. Sit tight — this is noise for a long-term holder.

watch_today.title: US-Iran tensions: watch oil prices and your US holdings
watch_today.detail: Trump threatened to bomb Oman overnight as the 60-day US-Iran ceasefire negotiation deadline expired with no deal. Iran has threatened a new offensive. Oil is currently at $84.28 — relatively contained for now, but an escalation could spike energy prices quickly, which would weigh on global markets including your VTS and VDHG holdings. Worth keeping an eye on this week.

watch_today.title: MSFT: Strong Q2 earnings — a positive signal
watch_today.detail: Microsoft was called out as one of the standout performers of the Q2 earnings season, alongside Palantir. MSFT's previous close is $495.40 USD. No price data yet for tonight's session, but the earnings momentum is a tailwind. For a long-term holder this is good news — the AI and cloud story at Microsoft is playing out well.

watch_today.title: TTWO: GTA 6 hype building — hold confidently
watch_today.detail: Take-Two Interactive held above $246 last session, with analysts noting that GTA 6-driven revenue expectations are lifting fiscal 2027 targets. Fan coverage is ramping up (Red Bull published a breakdown of every driveable vehicle teased so far). The GTA 6 launch thesis remains the core long-term reason to hold TTWO.

watch_today.title: AUD rising — good news for your Aussie purchasing power
watch_today.detail: The Australian dollar climbed to 71.09 US cents today — up 0.34%. Traders are now more confident the RBA won't raise interest rates, after consumer confidence improved following the RBA's rate pause. A stronger AUD slightly reduces the AUD value of your US-denominated holdings (GOOG, MSFT, TTWO) when converted back, but it's a minor effect at this level.

world.summary: The big global story today is the US-Iran war reaching a dangerous turning point as the 60-day ceasefire negotiation window slammed shut with no deal — and Trump is now threatening to bomb Oman. Elsewhere, geopolitical realignment in the Middle East is reshaping global alliances.

stories.title: Trump threatens to bomb Oman as US-Iran war hits stalemate
stories.why_it_matters: The 60-day window for US-Iran ceasefire negotiations has expired with no agreement, and Trump is now threatening military strikes on Oman — a country that has been acting as a diplomatic back-channel between Washington and Tehran. Iran has simultaneously threatened a new offensive. This puts the region on the brink of a major escalation. For everyday Australians, a broader Middle East conflict would likely spike oil prices (currently $84/barrel) and rattle global sharemarkets.

stories.title: Iran's secret plan to escalate the war
stories.why_it_matters: The Wall Street Journal reports Iran has a plan to significantly escalate its military campaign if negotiations remain stalled. Details are classified but the report suggests Iran is preparing new offensive capabilities. This raises the risk of a broader regional conflict involving US allies in the Gulf — a scenario that would have major consequences for global energy markets and economic stability.

stories.title: Iran threatens new offensive while US rules out extending ceasefire
stories.why_it_matters: The US has officially ruled out extending the ceasefire deadline, and Iran has responded by threatening a fresh military offensive. Reuters reports that the diplomatic window is now effectively closed. Both sides appear to be preparing for the next phase of a conflict that has already disrupted regional stability and kept oil markets on edge for months.

stories.title: The realignment of the Middle East
stories.why_it_matters: The Financial Times analyses how the US-Iran conflict is triggering a broader geopolitical realignment across the Middle East. Traditional alliances are shifting — some Gulf states are hedging their bets between Washington and other powers, while others are drawing closer to the US. The piece argues this reshaping of regional politics will have lasting consequences well beyond the immediate conflict.

stories.title: Trump's push to seize control of federal elections
stories.why_it_matters: With the clock ticking on his administration, Trump is intensifying efforts to give the federal executive branch more control over how US elections are run — a move that critics say would undermine the independence of state-run electoral systems. The Independent analyses how far Trump might push this before legal and political resistance stops him. For Australians, US political instability is a background risk to global markets and the reliability of American institutions.

politics.summary: Australian politics today was dominated by gambling ad reform, with Labor's bill set to pass — including a new opt-out register for online gambling ads. Separately, the RBA is in focus after a rate pause lifted consumer confidence, but the central bank is sounding alarms about state government debt.

stories.title: Labor's gambling ad bill set to pass, with opt-out register for Australians
stories.why_it_matters: Labor has struck a deal with the Coalition to pass its gambling advertising reform bill, with the key addition of a national opt-out register — meaning Australians will soon be able to sign up to stop receiving all gambling ads online. Independent Senator David Pocock has flagged concerns the bill doesn't go far enough, but it will pass regardless. This is a significant change for the millions of Australians who are currently bombarded with betting ads during live sport.

stories.title: Labor forced to scrap controversial 'widow tax'
stories.why_it_matters: After months of backlash, Labor has abandoned its so-called 'widow tax' — a policy that would have reduced superannuation death benefits paid to some surviving spouses. The backlash came from widows and retirees who argued the change would leave them worse off financially after losing a partner. The government has backed down entirely, meaning the current rules on super death benefits remain unchanged.

stories.title: Consumer confidence lifts after RBA rate pause
stories.why_it_matters: Australian consumer confidence has improved following the RBA's decision to hold interest rates steady at its last meeting. When households feel the Reserve Bank isn't going to make their mortgage repayments more expensive, they tend to loosen the purse strings a bit. This is a mild positive signal for the Australian economy — though the RBA hasn't ruled out future hikes if inflation proves sticky.

stories.title: RBA sounds alarm on state government debt binge
stories.why_it_matters: The Reserve Bank of Australia has flagged concern about the pace at which state governments are racking up debt. High state borrowing competes with private borrowing for the same pool of funds, which can push up interest rates and squeeze household finances. The RBA warning is a signal that even without raising the official cash rate, financial conditions could tighten if governments keep spending heavily.

ai.summary: Today's AI news is dominated by regulatory debates heating up globally — and a notable product launch from Alibaba taking aim at Meta's AI models.

stories.title: Alibaba launches laptop-ready AI model to challenge Meta
stories.why_it_matters: Alibaba has released a new AI model designed to run directly on a laptop — no cloud connection required. This is a direct challenge to Meta's locally-run AI models, which have been popular with developers who want AI tools that don't send data to external servers. Laptop-ready AI means your computer can run powerful AI tools privately and offline, which is a big deal for privacy-conscious users and businesses. The competition between Chinese and US AI labs is intensifying rapidly.

stories.title: AI regulation becoming a bottleneck for business — experts warn
stories.why_it_matters: A leading computer science journal is warning that as governments pile on AI rules, the regulations themselves are becoming a bottleneck that slows down the deployment of useful AI systems. Businesses face a patchwork of different rules in different countries, making it hard to roll out AI tools consistently. The concern is that over-regulation could hand an advantage to jurisdictions — like China — that are moving faster with fewer restrictions.

stories.title: Research calls for AI rules in finance to protect consumers
stories.why_it_matters: New research is urging regulators to introduce specific AI rules for the financial sector, arguing that consumers are at risk from AI systems making lending, insurance, and investment decisions without proper oversight. The concern is that AI can embed bias or make opaque decisions that disadvantage certain customers — and right now there are few rules stopping that from happening in finance specifically.

stories.title: AI model benchmark war: Claude Sonnet 5 vs GPT-5.6 vs Gemini 3.7 Flash
stories.why_it_matters: The latest round of AI model comparisons pits Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 5, OpenAI's GPT-5.6, and Google's Gemini 3.7 Flash head-to-head across a range of tasks. These benchmarks matter because they shape which AI tools businesses and developers choose to build on — and Google (GOOGL) and Microsoft (MSFT, via its OpenAI partnership) both have major stakes in this race. Staying current on which models lead the pack helps track the competitive landscape for your tech holdings.

sport.summary: NRL Round 25 is coming up this week, with team lists dropping today. The AFL Sydney Swans investigation into a sexual assault allegation is the biggest footy story outside the NRL, and there's a surprise Melbourne Storm signing to note.

stories.title: Manly's big Turbo call and Tigers' major team shake-up ahead of Round 25
stories.why_it_matters: Fox Sports reports Manly has a big selection call to make over Tom Trbojevic (Turbo) ahead of Round 25, while coach Madge is set to make major changes to the Wests Tigers lineup. The Dolphins host the Eels at Suncorp Stadium Friday night — a local Gold Coast-adjacent game worth watching. Cowboys have the bye this round.

stories.title: Melbourne Storm lock up surprise signing and poach key forward from Sydney rival
stories.why_it_matters: The Storm have made two significant roster moves ahead of 2027: a surprise re-signing (details not yet public) and the poaching of a key forward from an unnamed Sydney club. Melbourne are clearly building for another title tilt — bad news for the rest of the competition and particularly for Queensland clubs chasing a premiership.

stories.title: Sydney Swans players under investigation over sexual assault claim
stories.why_it_matters: Police are investigating a sexual assault allegation involving Sydney Swans AFL players. The ABC reports the AFL is also conducting its own investigation. AFL.com.au notes that Will Fraser has been flagged as 'ready' for a leadership role amid the turmoil — suggesting the club is managing significant internal disruption. This is a serious matter that has now attracted international media coverage via the BBC.

stories.title: AFL team whispers: Key Swan injured, Magpies and Suns also missing players
stories.why_it_matters: AFL team whispers ahead of this week's round reveal a key Sydney Swan is carrying an injury (adding to the club's off-field woes), Collingwood will be without at least one player, and a star Gold Coast Sun is ruled out. The Suns' injury news is directly relevant for Gold Coast fans — expect lineup changes when official teams drop Wednesday night.
